label: DOCUMENTED
headline: Mary: 1 in 13 girls
text: Named for the Virgin Mary, Christianity's most honored woman, Mary went to 7.8% of all US girls born in 1880. That's nearly triple #2 Anna.
image_credit: Sassoferrato, The Virgin in Prayer (1640s), public domain

label: THEORY
headline: Old-world classics rule
text: Bible, saints and royalty: Anna, Elizabeth, Margaret and Emma (heroine of Jane Austen's novel Emma). Many came over with European immigrants.
image_credit: Castle Garden immigrant depot, NY, Charles Magnus print, CC0

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: Nicknames on the birth certificate
text: Victorians loved cozy -ie names. Minnie (from Wilhelmina or Mary) and Bessie (from Elizabeth) were given as full names, not just pet names.

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: The Lady with the Lamp
text: Nurse Florence Nightingale, heroine of the Crimean War, made Florence a name of courage. She was named after her birthplace, Florence, Italy.
image_credit: Florence Nightingale, c.1857, Henry Hering, public domain

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: America's first celebrity baby
text: President Grover Cleveland's daughter "Baby Ruth" was born in Oct 1891 to a press frenzy. Ruth leapt from #46 in 1890 to #5 in 1892.
image_credit: Ruth Cleveland (1897), unknown photographer, public domain

label: THEORY
headline: Dorothy and the Wizard of Oz
text: Dorothy is the heroine of the 1900 children's book The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, a huge bestseller. Dorothy went from #35 in 1899 to #3 by 1915.
image_credit: W. W. Denslow, Wizard of Oz illustration (1900), public domain

label: THEORY
headline: Betty: the Roaring Twenties name
text: Once just a nickname for Elizabeth, Betty became a name of its own as silent-film stars like Betty Compson used it. #53 in 1915, #2 by 1928.
image_credit: Betty Compson, 1921, Alfred Cheney Johnston, public domain

label: THEORY
headline: Joan Crawford's Joan
text: In 1925 the MGM film studio renamed actress Lucille LeSueur "Joan Crawford." As she became a star, Joan shot from #41 in 1927 to #5 by 1931.
image_credit: Joan Crawford, 1928, Ruth Harriet Louise, public domain

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: Shirley Temple mania
text: Child film star Shirley Temple broke out in 1934 (Stand Up and Cheer!, Bright Eyes). Baby Shirleys nearly tripled: 14,000 in 1933, 42,000 in 1935.
image_credit: Shirley Temple, Bright Eyes (1934), Fox, public domain

label: THEORY
headline: Hollywood's Linda
text: Film actress Linda Darnell became a Hollywood star in 1939-40. Linda went from #49 in 1937 to #8 in 1940, jumping 71% in one year.
image_credit: Linda Darnell, 20th Century Fox publicity, public domain

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: A hit song makes Linda #1
text: Buddy Clark's 1947 hit song "Linda" was written for a lawyer's toddler: Linda Eastman, later Linda McCartney. Linda ended Mary's 67-year reign.
image_credit: Buddy Clark, c.1947, William P. Gottlieb/LoC, public domain

label: THEORY
headline: Deborah Kerr's Hollywood rise
text: British actress Deborah Kerr became a Hollywood star in the late 1940s. Deborah climbed from #62 in 1947 to #4 by 1951.
image_credit: Studio press photo (1958) / Public domain
image_caption: Deborah Kerr in a 1950s studio portrait

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: Mary takes back #1
text: Mary didn't surge; it was slowly slipping. Linda just crashed faster, from 4.7% of girls in 1950 to 3.3% in 1953, so Mary was back on top.
image_credit: Sassoferrato, The Virgin in Prayer (1640s), public domain

label: THEORY
headline: Lisa's climb to #1
text: Nat King Cole's 1950 hit song "Mona Lisa" (it won the Oscar for best film song) may have helped. Lisa went from #220 in 1950 to #1 by 1962.
image_credit: Nat King Cole, 1947, William P. Gottlieb/LoC, public domain

label: THEORY
headline: Kim Novak makes Kim a girl's name
text: Kim was mostly a boy's name until 1954, when film star Kim Novak (Picnic, Vertigo) made it feminine. Kimberly climbed from #22 to #2 by 1966.
image_credit: Kim Novak, Columbia Pictures still (1959), public domain

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: The Beatles sing "Michelle"
text: The Beatles' love song "Michelle" came out in Dec 1965 on the album Rubber Soul. In 1966 the name jumped from #18 to #4: 11,000 more girls.
image_credit: EMI publicity photo (1965) / Public domain
image_caption: The Beatles in 1965, the year they recorded Michelle

label: THEORY
headline: Love Story's Jenny
text: Jennifer was already climbing when Love Story, a bestselling 1970 novel and the year's biggest film, made Jenny a heroine. #1 for 15 years.
image_credit: Ali MacGraw, 1972 publicity photo, public domain
image_caption: Ali MacGraw, who played Jenny in the film

label: THEORY
headline: Mary drops out of the top 12
text: For the first time on record, Mary falls out of the top 12. Sociologists blame a shift from tradition to individuality, not just less religion.
image_credit: Sassoferrato, The Virgin in Prayer (1640s), public domain

label: THEORY
headline: Jessica: a name Shakespeare made up
text: Shakespeare invented Jessica for a character in his play The Merchant of Venice. Soft and Jennifer-like, it rose from #34 in 1973 to #1 in 1985.
image_credit: Luke Fildes, Jessica (1896), public domain

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: A soap opera makes Ashley
text: Once a boy's name, Ashley jumped from #17 to #4 in 1983, after rich heiress Ashley Abbott arrived on the TV soap opera The Young and the Restless.
image_credit: Eileen Davidson, photo by Mingle MediaTV (2014), CC BY-SA 2.0
image_caption: Eileen Davidson, who played Ashley Abbott

label: THEORY
headline: Who's the Boss? made Samantha
text: In 1984 the TV sitcom Who's the Boss? debuted, with tomboy daughter Samantha. The name tripled in 6 years, from #39 to #5.
image_credit: White House Photographic Office (Reagan Library) / Public domain

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: A mermaid named Madison
text: In the 1984 film comedy Splash, a mermaid picks her human name from a New York street sign: Madison Avenue. #78 in 1993, #3 by 2000.
image_credit: Cassidy Turner / CC BY-SA 3.0
image_caption: Daryl Hannah, who played Madison the mermaid in Splash (1984)

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: Friends: Rachel has baby Emma
text: On the TV sitcom Friends, Rachel and Ross named their baby Emma in May 2002. That year Emma jumped from #13 to #4, then reached #1.
image_credit: Gga2015 / CC BY-SA 4.0
image_caption: The real Central Perk set from Friends

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: Celebrity babies revive Ava
text: Only 285 baby Avas in 1996. Then actresses Heather Locklear and Reese Witherspoon named daughters Ava. By 2005 it was top 10.
image_credit: Ava Gardner, The Killers (1946) publicity photo, public domain
image_caption: Ava Gardner, the 1940s film star Reese's Ava is named after

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: Twilight's Bella takes #1
text: Bella Swan, heroine of the Twilight vampire novels (2005) and films (2008), is short for Isabella. Isabella hit #1 in 2009.
image_credit: Kristin Dos Santos / CC BY-SA 2.0
image_caption: Bella Swan on a New Moon poster, Comic-Con 2009

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: Sophia + Sofia = the real #1
text: Sophia hit #1 in 2011. Count the Spanish and Italian spelling Sofia too, and the name has beaten every official #1 since 2007.
image_credit: Sofía Vergara, photo by Keith Hinkle (2009), CC BY 2.0

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: Harper Seven Beckham
text: In July 2011, soccer star David Beckham and Victoria "Posh Spice" Beckham named their daughter Harper. It jumped from #120 to #10 by 2015.
image_credit: David & Victoria Beckham, Mike Fanshawe (2019), CC BY 3.0

label: THEORY
headline: Olivia's 45-year climb to #1
text: Singer Olivia Newton-John made it modern in the '70s; The Cosby Show's little Olivia (1989) nearly doubled it in a year. #1 since 2019.
image_credit: Bert Verhoeff/Anefo (1978), CC0

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: Charlotte closes in on #1
text: From #289 in 2000 to #2 in 2025. Princess Charlotte (born 2015) gave it a royal shine. In 2025 it finished just 144 babies behind Olivia.
image_caption: Princess Charlotte at Trooping the Colour, 2019
image_credit: Londisland (YouTube) / CC BY 3.0

label: DOCUMENTED
headline: Names are spreading out
text: 1880: #1 Mary = 7.8% of girls. 2025: #1 Olivia = 0.84%. Parents now want names that stand out. Will Charlotte take #1 in 2026?
